title.rendered: ALA webinar: state and territory biodiversity data systems – recent advances and future directions.

content.rendered:
Australia is one of the most biologically diverse places on Earth. From our larger states, like Western Australia and New South Wales, to our smallest, Tasmania, each has high levels of regional endemism with species which occur nowhere else.

All the states and territories have publicly available atlases of their biodiversity data, and they share versions of this data with the Atlas of Living Australia. Data from states and territories makes up around 20% of the biodiversity data in Australia. It’s particularly important for our national understanding of vertebrate animals and vascular plants.

The conservation agencies in Australia’s states and territories manage large biodiversity data holdings for a wide variety of purposes centred upon environmental management and approvals and meeting statutory obligations under the various pieces of legislation in their jurisdictions.

The ALA receives support from the Australian Government through the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and is hosted by CSIRO.

Presenters

Trisha Moriarty and Anshu Gupta

Dandjoo, Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), Biodiversity Information Office (BIO)

Ron Avery

NSW BioNet, Senior Team Leader, Biodiversity Information Systems,

David McElwee

Natural Values Atlas, Tasmania. Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania

Facilitator

Peggy Newman
Team Data Management Lead, Atlas of Living Australia

Peggy is the Data Manager at the ALA, and the Australian Node Manager of the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). She leads the Data Management team who map, ingest and index datasets from hundreds of data providers from the government, collections and citizen science sectors.

Q&A discussion

The conversation sparked so many great questions – more than we could fit into the session, so we’ve taken the time to answer the rest here.

State and transition simulation models are more likely to be used with vegetation coverage datasets than the biodiversity occurrence datasets. We’ve discussed at this webinar.

In the ALA, sensitive species locations are systematically obscured for all ingested data using generalisation rules captured in Sensitive Lists (see: https://lists.ala.org.au/?filters=isSDS:true) provided by states and territories, and Birdlife Australia. Culturally sensitive species locations are managed through data governance processes and decisions made together with data providers.

In the ALA using Darwin Core, data providers may use the occurrenceStatus field to nominate “present” or “absent” values for an occurrence.

Species occurrence data exists for many islands; however, the ALA does not hold extensive data on whether a species is flagged as invasive for a particular location. To study invasive species in an area, we recommend uploading a list of your target invasive species to the lists tool and using it to query occurrences.

Yes, Biodiversity Information Office (Dandjoo) is planning to look at IMSA data. The initial focus has been on terrestrial data from the IBSA portal with survey data from 356 projects ingested. Dandjoo currently holds marine data from providers such WA Museum, iNaturalist and Dept. Biodiversity Conservation and Attractions.

BioNet contains marine and aquatic species data but this data holding is not comprehensive

a. Does it mean that eventually there will be only one ALA site with appropriate state management.

b. Also for the future is there any standardisation of AI platforms used?

Each state provided budget information in a previous question.

In the foreseeable future it is unlikely that all state and territory atlases and the ALA will be merged, as each has differing jurisdictional responsibilities and funding arrangements.

To that end there is no standardisation of AI platforms.

a. Is there an alternative to digital systems (i.e. if systems go down)?

b. Who owns this data?

Data in the ALA, and on most modern government platforms, is managed onshore either on premise or in the cloud. Non sensitive data that is published through the ALA is also published to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).

Most modern IT systems are well managed for resilience to outages and disaster recovery.

Most of the data we discussed in the webinar is released publicly by data providers under Creative Commons licensing, and they would be the most likely to be named the “data owners”. With biodiversity data, there are often many parties involved with the collection and dissemination of data (data custodians, stewards, informaticians) and it’s important that users of data correctly follow the attribution requirements as set out by the Creative Commons license applied by the data provider.

Data flows from BioNet to the ALA and to GBIF, and there will be differences in the data primarily due to the different taxonomic backbones of all three. The ALA invites new data providers and provides tooling (Galaxias) and guidance for sharing data.

The new NVA interface will be live on 19 November.

BioNet will be publishing its large flora and fauna systematic survey data holding via a new web service in 2026. This data is complex containing information about the site, replicates, survey method, species census, and measurements for fact. This is the first step in a longer journey of refinement. To interpret species absence routinely from these datasets further work may be needed. Site locations will be made available as spatial layer.

In the NVA survey effort should be captured in the survey metadata for each survey. It isn’t a map of survey effort (hours per grid square). I appreciate that would be nice, but it isn’t what we are showing. It is a step in the direction that would get us to that destination though.

a. That’s a great point. And it would be great if some information on survey effort/coverage would be given in these databases. In my experience, the “survey sites” names that I’ve seen in downloaded data from BioNet and NVA seem to be a mix of established survey sites and incidental records or unknown survey effort/coverage, and where possible, I have used other fields to determine the type of record (incidental, standardised survey, etc.). And absolutely, absences are often not captured or captured in an inconsistent way. But I would love to hear from the BioNet and NVA teams here!

b. Thanks. It seems that survey effort is only captured in metadata for species presence records. I once tried to look at all small mammal records, and plot any that had ‘mammal trapping’ as a method to understand spatial coverage of targeted small mammal surveys. roundabout way to get there! Would be great if it was captured

In general, we accept that systematic survey data needs to be a focus of our systems.

BioNet delivers species observation data to ALA and Biodiversity Data Repository, but does not yet received data back, although this is evolving as a priority. Species absence is not codified; it is inferred from other information including method, effort, and timing of survey that is held in the systematic survey data model and metadata. Exposure of this systematic survey data via open web services is a first step and will allow us to test and refine our approach in future releases.

Dandjoo delivers species occurrence and systematic survey data to the federal Biodiversity Data Repository and non-sensitive data is also available through ALA. Most data in Dandjoo have a Creative Commons By Attribution licence, but there are small number of datasets that cannot be on shared due to licence constraints impose by the rightsholder.

The NVA has generally not recorded absences for things that were not previously known to be present on that site—giant trees, eagle nests etc might be recorded as absent; shore birds, wallabies, ephemeral plants et cetera would not.

There is also a difference between ‘absent’ and ‘not detected’. We are hoping to accommodate both.

Going forwards, we should be doing a better job of capturing presences and not detected/absence data in the new NVA, but it is not something that was well catered for in the old NVA as recording of survey method and effort were not well supported and without that these are only half the whole.

a. I was wondering how frequently BioNet data is uploaded to ALA. Also does all data feed to ALA or subset of data

All publicly available BioNet data (a subset of the total) is loaded to the ALA weekly.

Records in the ALA are reprocessed regularly to match the provided taxonomic details (name, higher taxonomic details) to the current accepted taxonomic name. Historical views of the taxonomic backbone are not retained.

excerpt.rendered: We invited representatives from Dandjoo in Western Australia, NSW BioNet and the Natural Values Atlas in Tasmania to showcase their respective repositories, recent advances and future directions.

content.rendered:
Welcome to the Atlas of Living Australia September 2026 newsletter

The Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) has recently released its 2026-27 Annual Work Plan, outlining an ambitious program of work to strengthen Australia’s national biodiversity data infrastructure and support the growing needs of researchers, governments, industry and the community. We are proud to share a plan that builds on the ALA Strategy 2025-2030, with a strong focus on improving biodiversity data quality and governance, supporting emerging data streams such as camera traps and acoustic monitoring, and advancing the transition to a modern, cloud-native platform.

The work plan also highlights investments in Indigenous partnerships, national research infrastructure collaborations including CoastRI, enhanced user experiences, and new analytical capabilities that will help turn biodiversity data into actionable insights. Together, these initiatives reinforce the ALA’s role as a trusted national asset supporting biodiversity science, conservation and evidence-based environmental decision-making across Australia.

The National Digital Research Infrastructure (NDRI) investment round has delivered a major boost for the ALA, with significant government funding secured over coming years to accelerate key national biodiversity data initiatives. Funded projects include the:

  • Next Generation Biodiversity Data Platform, which will modernise the ALA’s digital infrastructure and enhance access to biodiversity data at scale,
  • Building NDRI Capabilities with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Rangers and Knowledge Holders, a partnership with Curtin University, TERN, CSIRO and the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water that will strengthen Indigenous environmental data capabilities and support ranger-led biodiversity data management.

Alongside other NCRIS partnership projects funded under the National Digital Research Infrastructure Strategy, these investments will position the ALA to deliver next-generation biodiversity infrastructure while expanding access to nationally significant environmental data and supporting better research and decision-making outcomes.

Finally, I’d like to thank our users who contribute to the ALA annual user satisfaction survey, which is open at present. As a data driven organisation, we find your feedback and the metrics derived from it invaluable and your feedback does shape our project priorities, for example around data quality and enhancing our user experience (a major project currently underway). We’ve received some fantastic longitudinal data from the last few years of surveys so please do continue to share your perspectives, and experiences with the ALA.

Happy Biodiversity Month, and I hope you enjoy reading our September newsletter.

Andre Zerger
Director, ALA

title.rendered: Updated Species List tool now live

content.rendered:
The ALA Species List tool is now streamlined and easier to use.

This tool lets users make, upload and maintain a personalised list of species of interest. This can be used either manually or via an API within or external to ALA data.

Project Manager for the Lists Upgrade, Tania Laity, said it’s now easier to update and query lists.

“We’ve upgraded the front end, so it’s more intuitive for users and more useful,” Tania said.

“That’s probably the key point.”

What does the List tool do?

The lists tool forms the core of how the ALA manages restricted access species data and how we apply obfuscations to records to protect sensitive species data. 

We use Lists to store the threatened species lists from states and territories, and add their threat status to the species pages and location data.

“The two main things people are looking to find are the conservation lists—the threatened species lists from all the States and Territories—and the sensitive species lists,” Tania said.

The lists tool brings all these lists together in one place—instead of having to go to individual websites to find each list.

It’s also used to add taxa to the taxonomy that aren’t yet included in other taxonomic sources and for Biosecurity Alerts, which uses lists to send alerts of sightings of invasive species to biosecurity agencies.

Using Lists for searching

Rather than undertaking quite complex queries of applying multiple filters to select particular species, users can create a list of the exact species of interest and use it like a query.

“If you create a list for the species you’re interested in, you can open the list and view all the records for those species,” Tania said.

The lists tool is also used in the spatial portal by industry users like environmental consultants to search for threatened species, or particular threatened species, in an area where they’re doing an environmental assessment.

Checking it twice

A big part of the project was helping users find the right lists and understand how to use them to query the data.

“The beginning of the process was to identify all important lists that are used in ALA tools and systems,” Tania said.

For lists created in Spatial Portal the default setting had previously been to make them public.

“It was generating all these lists, which was confusing if someone was just looking for the authoritative threatened species list, as they would have to search through thousands of lists to try to find the right one” Tania said.

“We’ve now made them private by default so the people who created them can still use them if they want to by logging in,” Tania said.

Now when users create a list, it will automatically be set to private.

Faster, fresher and focused on the future

The refreshed lists tool has an updated user interface, and it’s faster.

“There used to be a limit on how many species it would query when you went to view all records, but now it views everything,” Tania says.

“So you can put in quite a big list, say a few thousand species, and it will now show all records for all of those species.”

“And it’s easier for other users to search and find the lists they are looking for, such as conservation lists.”

The next phase of the project will look at better governance processes for lists.

There’ll be more tidying up and reclassifying, and clearer processes to manage lists and make them more understandable for users.

“The aim is to make it as easy as possible for people to search and find the list they want!”

title.rendered: Where there’s a will, there’s a Quail – ALA data now natively in QGIS

content.rendered:
We’ve released Quail, a new plugin for the QGIS geospatial program.

Quail enables users to locate and download species occurrence records (observations, specimens, eDNA records, etc.), and to narrow their queries to particular taxa, locations or times.

Users can also filter their queries based on threatened and sensitive species lists or to meet particular data-quality criteria. These data are then read into QGIS as a vector layer.

Quail was built and is maintained by Amanda Buyan, a member of our Science & Decision Support Team. We found out more from Amanda about this new tool.

What is QGIS and how is it used?

QGIS is a free and popular software program for creating, editing and visualising geospatial information. Ecologists will often use maps of known or historical species observations as valuable context for scientific research, conservation management, environmental impact assessments and decision making.

Many ecologists need a tool to visualise species onto a map outside of a programming interface, and QGIS is the natural choice for a mapping software. QGIS also has an advantage in the form of ‘plugins’ – bespoke programs designed to analyse or import data directly into QGIS.

There are several existing QGIS Plugins for downloading biodiversity data. Although each plugin has their strengths, they remain limited in their filtering functionality and data scope.

Quail aims to address these limitations by offering a QGIS interface to download biodiversity data using a complete set of taxonomic, temporal and spatial filtering options, including the option to download data natively from GBIF, the Atlas of Living Australia and 7 other Living Atlases.

How can researchers use Quail?

Researchers can use Quail to download species occurrences for use in initial ecological assessments (i.e. to get an idea of where a species exists, or what kinds of species are in an area) before carrying out field research. They can also input this data into a species distribution model, which predicts the likelihood of seeing a particular species in an area.

Others will be using it to carry out initial ecological assessments of an area potentially slated for mining or land development, and this can provide an initial insight into what species have been seen in a particular area.

Watch the video: Intro to Quail

What inspired the name: Quail?

We chose Quail because we wanted to have a species that is represented in many countries; however, being part of the Atlas of Living Australia, we wanted to highlight a native Australian quail! The one we have chosen is the Eastern King Quail (Synoicus chinesis victoriae), as it is endangered in Victoria and South Australia, and a beautiful species.

How does Quail make data more usable/searchable?

Quail makes data more searchable/usable by offering greater flexibility in how users can query data, be it spatially, temporally or taxonomically. We have been building towards this for a while. Quail is built on galah, our R and Python packages for flexibly extracting data out of the ALA into a programming environment.

As there are users that want this flexibility but may not have the time to learn to code, we chose to create a QGIS plugin that gives users the ability to view occurrence data on a map and in context without having to go to many sources and/or manually upload data downloaded from the ALA website.

What will the impact be?

Quail will bring greater visibility and accessibility to data from the ALA, as well as several other atlases. More users can access biodiversity data directly in QGIS, streamlining and speeding up their ecological assessments and analysis.

What are you most proud of with this new release?

I’m most proud of the overall design of the plugin. I have attempted to add as much flexibility as I could within a relatively minimal, easy-to-use interface.

What’s been the best part about working on the project?

The best part about working on this project has been seeing the flexibility that I know galah offers come to life in the user interface of this new plugin in a geospatial focussed environment. It provides a new way to access ALA data in a widely used, external map-based interface.

How did the team work make the dream work?

I created and led the lion’s share of the project. However, the plugin wouldn’t be where it is today without the helpful suggestions and feedback at various stages from Dax Kellie, Shandiya Balusabramaniam, Juliet Seers, Tania Laity and Cameron Slatyer. Thanks to all of them for helping our Quail take flight!

What are you most looking forward to seeing around impact?

I’m most looking forward to seeing how it will assist users in industry, government and other decision-making roles to deliver real world impact.

Watch the video: Intro to Quail

Find out more at: https://quail.ala.org.au/
